# The Compute Frontier: Bandwidth, Not FLOPs {#sec-compute-frontier}

@sec-accelerators-networking taught the reader to read a cluster as three
bandwidth tiers and to diagnose a run with one honest number, model FLOPs
utilization. That chapter described how the tiers work. This one asks where
each tier breaks. By the end a reader can say why the scarce resource at the
frontier is bytes rather than arithmetic, why a single accelerator is now a
package of chiplets rather than one die, why the NVLink boundary that the
earlier chapter pinned to a node has moved to a whole rack, and which of the
escape routes from the bandwidth wall are already shipping rather than
promised.

## A spec sheet that lies in the same direction every year

A frontier accelerator's datasheet leads with a peak arithmetic rate, and
the rate climbs fast across generations, faster still once the precision
drops from FP16 to FP8 to FP4. Read only that line and the machine looks
like it is getting better at the thing training and inference need most.
The line is true and almost beside the point. The work a transformer does is
not bound by how fast the multiply-accumulate units can run; it is bound by
how fast operands reach them. Attention decode, mixture-of-experts routing,
and any kernel that touches more memory than it reuses spend their time
waiting on high-bandwidth memory, not on the matrix units. The roofline of
@sec-accelerators-networking already named this: below a kernel's arithmetic
intensity the achievable rate is set by HBM bandwidth, and the peak FLOPs
ceiling is unreachable.

The frontier problem is that the two numbers on the roofline diverge. Across
recent accelerator generations, low-precision matrix throughput has climbed
much faster than HBM bandwidth per chip. Stating the trend honestly matters
more than a headline multiple: from the V100 era to Blackwell, peak compute
grew by roughly an order of magnitude more than memory bandwidth did, and the
recent FP4 and FP8 jumps widen the gap further because they multiply
arithmetic throughput without moving a single byte faster. The arithmetic
intensity a kernel must reach to escape the memory-bound region therefore
rises every generation. This is the memory wall, and it is not a temporary
manufacturing lag. It is the structural fact that organizes the whole
chapter: every tier of the machine, the chip, the package, the rack, and the
power behind them, is hitting a ceiling that bandwidth, not arithmetic, sets.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-compute-frontier-walls
%%| fig-cap: "The frontier as a stack of ceilings, each binding at a different tier. The spec sheet's FLOPs sits at the bottom and is the least scarce; bytes, package area, fabric reach, and megawatts bind above it."
flowchart TB
  flops["peak FLOPs<br/>(spec-sheet headline, least scarce)"]
  hbm["HBM bandwidth + capacity<br/>(the memory wall)"]
  retic["reticle limit 858 mm²<br/>(forces chiplets on an interposer)"]
  fabric["scale-up fabric reach<br/>(how much silicon one coherent domain spans)"]
  power["power + cooling<br/>(the datacenter ceiling, @sec-powering-ai)"]
  flops --> hbm --> retic --> fabric --> power
```

## The chip: a die too small for its own memory

The innermost ceiling is geometric. A photolithography scanner can expose at
most one reticle field per shot, capped near 858 mm² [@shilov2026cowos]. A
frontier compute die already presses against that limit, so the only way to
add transistors is to stop building one die. Modern accelerators are several
compute chiplets and a row of HBM stacks tiled side by side on a silicon
interposer, the CoWoS (chip-on-wafer-on-substrate) package. The interposer,
not the logic die, is now the object whose area sets how much compute and how
many memory stacks one accelerator can carry. @sec-making-silicon owns the
question of whether that interposer can be fabricated and bought; here it is
enough to see that the reticle limit pushed packaging up into the
architecture, making interposer area a first-class design parameter.

What gets tiled onto the interposer is mostly memory, and the memory is the
point. NVIDIA's Rubin generation reaches roughly 288 GB of HBM4 at about
22 TB/s per accelerator. Google's Ironwood, the TPU v7, carries 192 GB of
HBM3e at 7.37 TB/s and is the first TPU to support FP8 natively rather than
through emulation [@google2025ironwood]. The numbers move every quarter, and
any specific figure in this chapter is a date stamp rather than a constant.
The durable observation is the ratio: capacity and bandwidth grow, but they
grow more slowly than the arithmetic that consumes them, so the fraction of
real workloads that are memory-bound rises over time.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow

HBM bandwidth growing slower than low-precision matrix throughput sets a
falling arithmetic-intensity floor. That floor dictates choices two layers
up: an ever-larger share of inference kernels land in the memory-bound region,
which is why the serving layer leans on FP8 and FP4 weights and on aggressive
key-value-cache management rather than on more FLOPs (cross-ref
@sec-memory-scheduling and @sec-quantization-kernels). Adding arithmetic to a
bandwidth-bound kernel buys nothing.
:::

## The rack: the scale-up boundary that moved

@sec-accelerators-networking drew a hard line at the node: tensor parallelism,
the most communication-hungry axis, had to stay inside the NVLink domain,
and that domain was the eight or so accelerators in one chassis. That line has
moved. The defining hardware shift of this generation is the deliberate
expansion of the coherent scale-up domain from a node to a whole rack.
NVIDIA's GB200 and GB300 NVL72 wire seventy-two GPUs into a single
NVLink-coherent domain spanning the rack, and the Rubin NVL72 keeps the form
factor while roughly doubling the fabric bandwidth. The rule from Part VII
still holds, but its boundary is now the rack rather than the chassis: tensor
parallelism stays inside the NVLink domain, and the domain got an order of
magnitude larger.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-compute-frontier-domain
//| fig-cap: "The scale-up domain that @sec-accelerators-networking pinned to a node has expanded to a rack. The most bandwidth-hungry parallelism axis can now span 72 accelerators inside one coherent fabric, where before it spanned roughly 8."
digraph scaleup {
  rankdir=LR;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1", penwidth=1.1];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280"];

  old [label="2023 scale-up domain\n~8 GPUs, one chassis\nTP fits here"];
  new [label="2026 scale-up domain\n72 GPUs, one rack (NVL72)\nTP fits here", color="#3b82f6", fontcolor="#3b82f6", penwidth=1.4];
  out [label="scale-out\nDP / PP across racks\nInfiniBand / Ethernet"];

  old -> new [label="NVLink domain\nblown open to rack scale"];
  new -> out [label="cheaper bytes\nsparse communication only"];
}
```

Why expand the domain at all? Because the memory wall and the parallelism
math interact. A larger coherent domain lets a model's tensor-parallel and
expert-parallel groups span more silicon at full fabric bandwidth, so the
per-device memory pressure of a trillion-parameter model is spread without
spilling the hungriest collective onto the slow inter-rack network. The rack
became the unit of frontier compute because that is the largest blast radius
the fabric can still hide a collective inside.

The expansion is not free, and copper is running out of reach. Past a rack,
the per-interface power of pluggable optical transceivers, on the order of
tens of watts each, becomes a budget the rack cannot spend. Co-packaged
optics move the fiber onto the switch package and cut the per-interface power
roughly from 30 W to 9 W, which is the case NVIDIA makes for Quantum-X and
Spectrum-X co-packaged switches shipping through 2026 [@nvidia2025cpo].
Beyond a fixed topology, optical circuit switching lets the fabric itself be
reconfigured per training phase; recent work on parallelism-driven optical
rails reports large network-power and cost reductions at a few percent
training overhead [@ding2026opus]. The through-line is that the fabric's
energy budget, not only its bandwidth, now bounds how large a coherent domain
can be built and cooled, which is the thread @sec-powering-ai picks up.

## The silicon menagerie: who is betting on bandwidth

For most of the deep-learning era the merchant GPU was the only serious
frontier accelerator, and its software ecosystem was the moat. The bandwidth
wall has opened room for a wider menagerie, and reading the entrants by what
they optimize is more instructive than ranking them by peak FLOPs.

The custom-ASIC bet is vertical integration: co-design the chip with the
network and skip the merchant margin. Google's Ironwood scales to a
9,216-chip superpod wired as a torus with optical circuit switches rather
than a switched fat-tree, and targets the inference-dominated workload mix
directly [@google2025ironwood]. Amazon's Trainium makes the same wager for
its own fleet. The merchant counter is AMD's memory-density play: its
rack-scale Helios system pairs accelerators carrying substantially more HBM
than the NVIDIA part it competes with, trading peak FP4 throughput for memory
capacity and bandwidth on the thesis that the wall is bytes, not arithmetic.
Under export controls, Huawei's CloudMatrix knits hundreds of domestic NPUs
into one optically-meshed scale-up domain that reaches frontier aggregate
bandwidth by brute force and roughly four times the power, a reminder that
the scale-up-domain idea is general and that the memory wall can be answered
with watts when the best silicon is unavailable.

At the contrarian edge sits wafer-scale. Cerebras keeps an entire model's
weights in on-die SRAM across a single wafer of 900,000 cores, with no HBM to
stream from, and reports multiples of GPU per-user token rate on
latency-bound decode [@cerebras2024wse3]. It is the purest bet against the
memory wall: if you never leave the die, there is no HBM bandwidth to be
bound by. Its ceiling is capacity, since on-wafer SRAM cannot hold a
trillion-parameter model, so it wins latency-bound serving rather than the
largest training runs.

## Escape routes, in order of maturity

The chapter's payoff is to sort the ways out of the bandwidth wall by how real
they are today, because the field's discourse mixes shipping hardware with
research slides.

Shipping now is rack-scale copper: the NVL72-class domain is in production and
is the reason tensor parallelism can span seventy-two devices. Shipping
through 2026 is co-packaged optics, the next step once copper runs out of
reach past the rack [@nvidia2025cpo]. A numeric escape route is already in
training pipelines: four-bit pretraining formats such as NVFP4 relax the
arithmetic-intensity floor by halving operand bytes while preserving accuracy
over multi-trillion-token runs, which is the cleanest way to make a
memory-bound kernel less memory-bound without new silicon (the format
mechanics belong to @sec-quantization-kernels). A structural route is to split
the workload across chips specialized for each phase: prefill is
compute-bound and tolerates cheaper high-capacity memory, while decode is
bandwidth-bound and wants scarce HBM, so a separate prefill-optimized class of
accelerator pairs with HBM parts for decode. That this idea has wavered in and
out of vendor roadmaps is itself a frontier-uncertainty signal worth
recording rather than smoothing over. Further out sit reconfigurable optical
fabrics [@ding2026opus] and wafer-scale integration [@cerebras2024wse3], real
research with real demonstrations but not yet the default.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-compute-frontier-escapes
//| fig-cap: "Escape routes from the bandwidth wall, ordered by maturity. The left column is in production; the right column is demonstrated but not default."

  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1", penwidth=1.1];
  edge [color="#6b7280"];

  subgraph cluster_ship { label="shipping"; color="#6b7280"; fontname="Helvetica"; fontsize=10;
    rack [label="rack-scale copper\n(NVL72 domain)"];

```

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested

Four debates are genuinely live, and the camps disagree on which non-FLOPs
wall binds first rather than on whether FLOPs stopped being the limit.

- **One coherent fabric, an open standard, or cheap Ethernet?** NVIDIA bets
  ever-larger proprietary NVLink domains are worth their cost. The UALink
  consortium wants an open switched standard to commoditize the scale-up tier.
  A pragmatist camp reuses Ethernet switch silicon for scale-up. Through 2026
  the pragmatists shipped first, because rack vendors fell back to
  Ethernet-substrate fabrics when native open-standard switch silicon was not
  yet available. NVIDIA has meanwhile partially opened its own fabric to
  third-party silicon, blurring the proprietary-versus-open line.
- **Is co-packaged optics mandatory or a reliability risk?** Proponents say
  copper is out of runway past a rack and optics is the only way to scale the
  domain. Skeptics point to unproven laser reliability and repairability at
  fleet scale and defend copper inside the rack. The dividing line is
  distance.
- **Do custom ASICs displace the merchant GPU?** The vertical-integration camp
  says co-designed silicon wins perf-per-watt on the inference-heavy mix. The
  incumbent camp says the software ecosystem and flexibility keep the GPU the
  default, and ASICs win only captive first-party workloads.
- **Is wafer-scale the answer or a niche?** It clearly wins latency-bound
  single-user decode and clearly cannot hold the largest models in SRAM. The
  unresolved question is whether model sizes plateau enough for on-die
  capacity to catch up.
:::

## Reading the frontier

The capability, efficiency, trust lens closes the chapter as it closes the
others. Capability at this layer is no longer set by how many FLOPs a chip can
retire but by how many bytes it can move and how much coherent silicon one
fabric can span, which is why the rack replaced the chip as the unit of
frontier compute. Efficiency moved into the numerics and the network: a
four-bit operand and a nine-watt optical interface buy more frontier than a
faster matrix unit, because both attack bytes rather than arithmetic. Trust,
at the silicon layer, is supply and concentration: a frontier run now depends
on whether a handful of buyers can secure interposer area and HBM stacks at
all, which is the allocation gate @sec-making-silicon takes up next. The
spec-sheet FLOPs was never the scarce resource. The scarce resources are
bytes, package area, fabric reach, and the megawatts behind them, and the
rest of this part follows that scarcity up the stack.
